sections: Welcome

Someone answers the phone. Someone knows where the file is. Someone set up the meeting and made sure everyone had what they needed. In many offices, that person is the administrative assistant.

This career mixes computer work, people skills, and organization. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is an Administrative Assistant?

You help an office run smoothly. You answer phones and greet visitors, keep calendars, prepare documents, and keep files in order. You might work for one boss or for a whole team.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Answer phones, take messages, and send calls to the right person.
  • Greet visitors and help them find what they need.
  • Schedule and confirm appointments and meetings.
  • Type letters, notes, and short reports.
  • Enter information into computer systems and keep files organized.
  • Order supplies and arrange repairs for office equipment.

The real picture: The job changes a lot from one office to the next. A school office, a clinic, a farm cooperative, and a state agency all need administrative help, but the details and the pace are different.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every office runs on its own schedule.

  • Morning: Check email and voicemail, then look at today's calendar.
  • Later: Greet a visitor, answer several calls, and fix a scheduling mix-up.
  • Midday: Print and put together packets for an afternoon meeting.
  • Afternoon: Enter information into a database and file the paperwork.
  • Before leaving: Write down what is unfinished and set up tomorrow's first tasks.

Some days are quiet. Others bring many interruptions at once. Learning to keep a list and come back to a task is part of the job.
How You Learn the Job

A four-year degree is not the usual entry route. About half of the people in this job say a high school diploma or GED is what the job needs. Many learn the office's systems on the job. Some employers ask for an associate degree or office experience, so read the actual job ad.

  • Build basic skills first: Typing, email, a calendar, word processing, and a simple spreadsheet. The programs offices list most are Microsoft Outlook, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
  • Start nearby: A receptionist, front desk, or office clerk job can lead to administrative work.
  • On-the-job training: Each office teaches its own phone system, records, and rules.
  • Optional education: North Dakota schools offering administrative assistant certificates or associate degrees include Bismarck State College, Cankdeska Cikana Community College in Fort Totten, Dickinson State University, Dakota College at Bottineau, Williston State College, and Rasmussen University in Fargo. Compare cost, length, and whether classes are online.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed for general administrative assistant work. Some specialized roles have their own rules. Requirements depend on the employer. Ask what you need to start.

  • Comfort with a computer, email, and common office programs.
  • Clear phone manners and careful spelling.
  • A background check for jobs in schools, clinics, banks, or government offices.
  • Training in the office's own systems, which the employer usually provides.
  • Optional office skills certificates; ask whether an employer actually wants one before you pay for it.

Before you begin: Ask who trains new staff, how long training lasts, and who you can go to with questions.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota administrative assistant pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $22.83 an hour ($47,480 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $19.36 and $25.91 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $16.79 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $29.22.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 6,490 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 6,640 in 2034, a change of +2%. That works out to about 720 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Schools, clinics, government offices, farm and energy companies, banks, churches, and almost every kind of business.

Work setting: Usually an office desk with a computer and phone. Many jobs are weekday, daytime hours. Some offices need part-time or early coverage.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, benefits, paid time off, training, and whether the job is full time, part time, or temporary.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced assistant: Handle more complicated scheduling, records, and projects.
  • Office manager: Lead the front office and other support staff as experience grows.
  • Specialized assistant: Medical, legal, or executive assistant roles may need extra training and often pay more.
  • A related direction: Bookkeeping, payroll, human resources, or customer service.

You can enjoy this work for a whole career without becoming a manager. Ask people in the office which paths are actually open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping people every day.
  • Indoor work with a regular schedule in many offices.
  • Jobs in almost every town and every kind of business.
  • Learning skills you can take to many other jobs.

Things to ask about:

  • Interruptions while you are trying to finish something.
  • Callers or visitors who are upset or in a hurry.
  • Long stretches of sitting and computer work.
  • Busy times with deadlines, such as the end of the month or a big meeting.

Across the country, the number of these jobs is projected to shrink. In North Dakota, the projection is close to flat with about 720 openings a year, mostly from people retiring or changing jobs.

A question for yourself: Do you like keeping things organized while helping the people around you?

sections: Welcome

Papers need filing. Mail needs sorting. Records need to be entered and found again later. Office clerks handle many of the tasks that keep an office running.

This job can be a first step into office work. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is an Office Clerk?

You do a mix of office tasks. You file and scan records, enter information into computers, sort mail, make copies, and answer questions at a counter or on the phone. The exact mix depends on the office.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • File, scan, and find paper and electronic records.
  • Enter information into computer systems and check it.
  • Sort and send mail and packages.
  • Make copies and prepare documents.
  • Answer phones and help people at a front counter.
  • Keep track of office supplies.

The real picture: Many clerk jobs are in government offices, schools, and large companies. Some are mostly computer work; others include more mail, counter work, or lifting boxes of records.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: The schedule depends on the office.

  • Morning: Sort the mail and deliver it to the right desks.
  • Later: Scan a stack of old paper records and check that each file saved correctly.
  • Midday: Help a person at the counter who needs a form.
  • Afternoon: Enter information from forms into a computer system.
  • Before leaving: Put away files and note what still needs to be done.

Some work is repetitive. Many clerks like knowing exactly what needs to be done and seeing a stack get smaller.
How You Learn the Job

Most office clerks learn on the job. Many employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Read the actual job ad for what each employer wants.

  • Build basic skills first: Typing, careful data entry, email, and a simple spreadsheet.
  • Practice accuracy: Getting names, dates, and numbers exactly right matters more than speed at first.
  • On-the-job training: Each office teaches its own filing system, forms, and computer programs.
  • Optional education: Short office skills or computer classes can help. Free classes may be available at libraries and job centers.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed for general office clerk work. Some specialized clerk jobs have their own rules. Ask the employer what you need to start.

  • Basic computer and typing skills.
  • Careful attention to detail.
  • A background check for some government, school, health, and bank jobs.
  • Training on privacy rules for the records you handle.
  • Some jobs include lifting mail bins or boxes; ask how much.

Before you begin: Ask who trains new staff and how you will know you are doing a task the right way.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota office clerk pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $24.11 an hour ($50,160 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $20.52 and $29.86 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $16.15 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $35.93.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 9,960 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 9,760 in 2034, a change of -2%. That works out to about 1,140 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: State, city, and county offices; schools and colleges; hospitals and clinics; banks; and large and small businesses.

Work setting: An office with a desk and computer, plus time at copiers, scanners, mail areas, or a front counter.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, benefits, paid time off, training, and whether the job is full time, part time, seasonal, or temporary.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced clerk: Take on more complicated records and special tasks.
  • Administrative assistant: Add scheduling, documents, and more contact with people.
  • Specialized clerk: Billing, payroll, bookkeeping, or medical records may need extra training.
  • Office supervisor: Lead other clerks as experience grows.

Working inside a school, hospital, or government office can also help you learn about other jobs there.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Clear tasks you can finish.
  • Indoor work with regular hours in many offices.
  • Jobs in many kinds of workplaces.
  • A way to learn how an organization works.

Things to ask about:

  • Repetitive tasks for long stretches.
  • Sitting and computer work for much of the day.
  • Lifting boxes or mail bins.
  • Busy times when many forms arrive at once.

North Dakota projects a small drop in office clerk jobs. There are still about 1,140 openings a year, mostly from people retiring or moving to other jobs.

A question for yourself: Do you like steady, careful work where you can see what you finished?

sections: Welcome

A customer comes in to deposit a paycheck, take out cash, or ask a question about an account. The bank teller helps them and makes sure every dollar is counted correctly.

This job mixes customer service and careful money handling. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Bank Teller?

You help customers with everyday banking at a counter or drive-up window. You take deposits, give out cash, cash checks, and answer questions. At the end of the day, your cash drawer has to match the computer exactly.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Take deposits and payments and give out cash.
  • Count money carefully and check it twice.
  • Use the bank's computer system for each transaction.
  • Check identification and follow security rules.
  • Answer questions and send customers to the right person for loans or new accounts.
  • Balance your cash drawer at the end of the day.

The real picture: Banks have strict rules, and tellers must follow them exactly. In small towns, tellers often get to know their customers well.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every branch has its own rhythm.

  • Morning: Count your cash drawer with a coworker before the doors open.
  • Later: Help a line of customers with deposits and withdrawals.
  • Midday: A business brings in a large deposit to count and record.
  • Afternoon: Answer phone questions and help at the drive-up window.
  • Before leaving: Balance your drawer so it matches the computer to the penny.

Fridays, paydays, and the first of the month can be busy. Some branches are open Saturday mornings.
How You Learn the Job

Most tellers learn on the job. About 7 in 10 people in this job say a high school diploma or GED is what new workers need. Many banks also want some cash handling or customer service experience. Read the actual job ad.

  • Build experience first: Cashier, retail, or customer service jobs teach counting money and helping customers.
  • Practice accuracy: Counting cash and checking your work matters more than speed.
  • On-the-job training: The bank teaches its computer system, security rules, and procedures, often for several weeks.
  • Optional education: Business or accounting classes can help if you want to move up in banking later.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed to be a teller. Banks have their own requirements. Ask what you need to start.

  • Comfort counting money and using a computer.
  • A background check; ask each employer what it checks.
  • Training in security, privacy, and fraud rules.
  • Clear, friendly communication with customers.
  • A schedule that may include Saturday mornings; ask.

Before you begin: Ask how long training lasts and who helps you when your drawer does not balance.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota teller pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $18.90 an hour ($39,300 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $18.27 and $22.04 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $17.84 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $22.97.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 1,970 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 1,770 in 2034, a change of -10%. That works out to about 180 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Banks, credit unions, and other financial businesses in cities and small towns across the state.

Work setting: A teller counter or drive-up window with a computer and cash drawer. Many tellers spend about half the day standing. The work is indoors with set opening hours.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, Saturday shifts, benefits, paid time off, training, and help paying for classes.
Where This Can Lead

• Head teller: Help other tellers and handle larger transactions.
  • Personal banker: Open accounts and help customers choose bank services.
  • Loan or operations work: Some tellers move into loan processing or back-office banking jobs.
  • A related direction: Bookkeeping, customer service, or office work.

Ask your employer whether they help pay for banking or business classes.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping people with something important to them.
  • Clear rules for how things are done.
  • Mostly daytime hours at many branches.
  • A possible first step into banking.

Things to ask about:

  • Standing at a counter for long periods.
  • Pressure to get every dollar exactly right.
  • Customers who are frustrated about their money.
  • Fewer teller jobs over time.

North Dakota expects about 10% fewer teller jobs over ten years, with about 180 openings a year. Pay is close together from beginner to experienced, so moving up often means moving into another banking role.

A question for yourself: Do you like helping people while being very careful with details?

sections: Welcome

A business sells something, pays a bill, and buys supplies. Someone has to record each of those and make sure it all adds up. That is the bookkeeper's job.

This career is about numbers, order, and careful checking. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Bookkeeping Clerk?

You keep a business's money records. You enter sales and bills into software, match receipts and bank statements, and find mistakes. Your records help owners and accountants make good decisions.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Record money coming in and going out.
  • Enter bills and invoices and track which are paid.
  • Match bank statements to the business's records.
  • Find and fix mistakes when numbers do not match.
  • Prepare simple reports for owners or accountants.
  • Keep financial files organized.

The real picture: In a small business, one bookkeeper may do everything. In a larger company, you might handle just one part, like bills or customer payments.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: The work follows the calendar.

  • Morning: Enter yesterday's sales and receipts into the bookkeeping software.
  • Later: Pay bills that are due this week and file the invoices.
  • Midday: Answer a question from a vendor about a payment.
  • Afternoon: Match the bank statement to the records and track down a small difference.
  • Before leaving: Note what is left before the end-of-month report.

The end of the month and tax time are often the busiest. Many bookkeepers like the quiet focus of the rest of the month.
How You Learn the Job

There is more than one way in. About 4 in 10 people in this job say a high school diploma or GED is what new workers need. About 1 in 5 say a short college certificate. Small businesses often train on the job. Read the actual job ad.

  • Build basic skills first: Spreadsheets, careful data entry, and basic math with percentages.
  • Learn the software: Many employers use QuickBooks or similar programs.
  • Optional education: North Dakota schools offering accounting technology or bookkeeping certificates and associate degrees include Williston State College, Dickinson State University, Bismarck State College, Turtle Mountain College in Belcourt, Dakota College at Bottineau, Minot State University, and Rasmussen University in Fargo.
  • On-the-job training: Each business has its own way of organizing its books.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed to be a bookkeeper. Requirements depend on the employer. Ask what you need to start.

  • Comfort with spreadsheets and numbers.
  • Experience with bookkeeping software, or willingness to learn it.
  • A background check for some jobs.
  • Care with private financial information.
  • Optional bookkeeping certifications; ask whether an employer values one before you pay for it.

Before you begin: Ask who reviews your work at first and who you go to when numbers do not match.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota bookkeeping clerk pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $23.90 an hour ($49,710 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $21.52 and $28.36 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $17.95 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $31.75.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 4,440 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 4,330 in 2034, a change of -3%. That works out to about 490 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Small businesses, farms and ranches, accounting offices, clinics, schools, nonprofits, and government offices.

Work setting: An office desk with a computer. Some jobs are part time or can be partly remote once you are trained.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, busy seasons, benefits, paid time off, training, and help paying for classes.
Where This Can Lead

• Full-charge bookkeeper: Handle all of a small business's books.
  • Payroll: Specialize in paying employees correctly.
  • Accountant: A bachelor's degree in accounting can lead to accountant jobs.
  • Office manager: Combine bookkeeping with running the office.

Some bookkeepers work for themselves and keep books for several small businesses.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Work where things add up and you can check them.
  • Quiet, focused tasks.
  • Jobs in many kinds of businesses, including farms and ranches.
  • A path toward accounting.

Things to ask about:

  • Long stretches at a computer.
  • Busy deadlines at month end and tax time.
  • Hunting for a small mistake that throws everything off.
  • Changes in software and how the work is done.

North Dakota expects a small drop in these jobs over ten years, with about 490 openings a year, mostly from retirements and job changes.

sections: Welcome

Payday matters to everyone. Behind each paycheck, someone checked the hours, figured the taxes and deductions, and made sure the money went out on time. That is payroll.

This career mixes numbers, rules, and helping workers understand their pay. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Payroll Clerk?

You make sure employees are paid correctly. You check hours and time sheets, enter pay changes, run payroll in software, and answer workers' questions about their paychecks.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Check hours worked, time off, and overtime.
  • Enter new workers and pay changes into the payroll system.
  • Figure pay, taxes, and deductions using payroll software.
  • Fix mistakes before paychecks go out.
  • Prepare reports and match payroll to bank records.
  • Answer workers' questions about their pay.

The real picture: Payroll runs on firm deadlines. A mistake affects a real person's paycheck, so careful checking matters every time.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: The week follows the pay schedule.

  • Morning: Collect time sheets and check for missing hours.
  • Later: Enter a new hire, a raise, and a change to someone's tax form.
  • Midday: A worker stops by because their overtime looks wrong. Look it up and explain it.
  • Afternoon: Run a payroll preview and check it line by line.
  • Before leaving: List anything that must be fixed before payroll is final.

The days before payday are busy. The end of the year brings extra tax forms.
How You Learn the Job

Many people come to payroll from other office work. Employers often look for bookkeeping, office, or human resources experience. Some ask for a college degree, so read the actual job ad.

  • Build basic skills first: Spreadsheets, careful data entry, and basic math with percentages.
  • Start nearby: Bookkeeping, office clerk, or human resources assistant jobs can lead to payroll.
  • Learn the software: Employers use payroll systems such as ADP, Workday, or Kronos. Each employer trains its own system.
  • Optional certification: PayrollOrg offers the Fundamental Payroll Certification for people new to payroll. Its website lists no experience requirement. Check the current cost and requirements on the PayrollOrg website.
  • Optional education: Accounting, business, or human resources classes at a North Dakota college can help.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed to do payroll. Requirements depend on the employer. Ask what you need to start.

  • Comfort with spreadsheets and numbers.
  • Experience with payroll or bookkeeping software, or willingness to learn it.
  • A background check for many jobs.
  • Strict care with private pay and tax information.
  • Willingness to keep learning as tax and wage rules change.

Before you begin: Ask who checks your work at first and who you go to with a tax or rule question.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota payroll clerk pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $29.13 an hour ($60,600 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $25.75 and $31.81 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $22.54 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $37.28.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 300 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 280 in 2034, a change of -9%. That works out to about 30 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Hospitals, manufacturers, school districts, government offices, larger businesses, and payroll service companies.

Work setting: An office desk with a computer. Some jobs can be partly remote once you are trained.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, benefits, paid time off, training, and help paying for a certification.
Where This Can Lead

• Payroll specialist: Handle more complex payroll, such as several states or many workers.
  • Payroll manager: Lead payroll for a larger employer.
  • Human resources: Payroll knowledge is useful in benefits and human resources jobs.
  • Accounting: More education can lead to accounting work.

Payroll companies also hire people to run payroll for many smaller businesses.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Clear rules and a clear right answer.
  • Knowing that people count on your work.
  • Pay that is higher than many entry-level office jobs.
  • Skills that connect to human resources and accounting.

Things to ask about:

  • Firm deadlines every pay period.
  • Workers who are upset when a paycheck looks wrong.
  • Rules that change and need to be learned.
  • Very few jobs with this exact title in North Dakota.

North Dakota has only about 300 payroll clerk jobs and about 30 openings a year. Payroll skills are still useful, because many bookkeepers, office managers, and human resources workers run payroll as part of their job.

A question for yourself: Do you like careful number work where getting it right helps people directly?

sections: Welcome

A patient calls to make an appointment. Another walks in and needs to check in. A doctor needs a record sent to a specialist. The medical secretary helps keep all of it moving.

This career is a way to work in healthcare from the office side. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Medical Secretary?

You handle the office work of a clinic, hospital department, or dental office. You schedule appointments, check patients in, handle insurance information, and keep medical records organized and private.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Answer phones and schedule appointments, tests, and procedures.
  • Greet and check in patients.
  • Collect and enter insurance information.
  • Send and receive medical records and test results.
  • Help patients fill out forms.
  • Keep patient information private and secure.

The real picture: You will see people who are sick, hurting, or worried. A calm, kind voice is part of the job.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Clinics are busiest when the doors open.

  • Morning: Check in a line of patients and scan their insurance cards.
  • Later: Answer calls and fit a sick patient into a full schedule.
  • Midday: Send records to a specialist and file test results.
  • Afternoon: Call patients to confirm tomorrow's appointments.
  • Before leaving: Check that tomorrow's schedule and paperwork are ready.

Some clinics have early, evening, or weekend hours.
How You Learn the Job

There is more than one way in. About half the people in this job say a high school diploma or GED is what new workers need. Others say an associate degree or a college certificate. Read the actual job ad.

  • Build basic skills first: Typing, email, scheduling, and clear phone manners.
  • Learn medical words: A medical terminology class helps you understand what doctors and nurses write.
  • Optional education: North Dakota schools with medical office programs include Turtle Mountain College in Belcourt, Dakota College at Bottineau, Bismarck State College, Williston State College, and Rasmussen University in Fargo.
  • On-the-job training: Each clinic trains staff on its own scheduling and records system.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

No state license is needed for this job. Employers set their own requirements. Ask what you need to start.

  • Comfort with a computer, phone, and scheduling software.
  • Training on patient privacy rules, which employers provide.
  • A background check, which many healthcare employers require.
  • Some employers ask for proof of certain vaccinations.
  • Optional medical office certifications; ask whether an employer wants one before you pay for it.

Before you begin: Ask how long training lasts and who helps with insurance and billing questions.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota medical secretary pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $21.82 an hour ($45,390 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $18.96 and $24.14 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $18.00 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $27.95.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 970 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 1,030 in 2034, a change of +6%. That works out to about 100 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Clinics, hospitals, dental offices, nursing homes, and other healthcare offices.

Work setting: A front desk or back office with a computer and phone, in a clean indoor setting.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, hours, weekend or evening shifts, benefits, paid time off, training, and help paying for classes.
Where This Can Lead

• Lead front office worker: Train new staff and handle harder scheduling problems.
  • Medical records or billing: More training can lead to medical records specialist or billing jobs.
  • Office manager: Run a clinic's front office as experience grows.
  • Patient care: Some people decide they want hands-on care and train as a medical assistant or nurse.

Ask your employer whether they help pay for healthcare classes.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Being part of healthcare without hands-on care.
  • Helping people when they need it.
  • Clinics and hospitals in many North Dakota towns.
  • A field that is expected to grow.

Things to ask about:

  • Busy phones and several requests at once.
  • Patients who are scared, in pain, or frustrated.
  • Long stretches of sitting and computer work.
  • Insurance rules that take time to learn.

North Dakota expects about 6% growth over ten years, with about 100 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Do you like staying organized and kind when things get busy?

sections: Welcome

A prescription comes in. Someone has to check it, count or measure the medicine, label it, and have it ready for the pharmacist to check. Pharmacy technicians do much of that work.

This career is a way into healthcare that needs careful, exact work. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Pharmacy Technician?

You help a pharmacist prepare and hand out medicine. You enter prescriptions into the computer, count or measure medicine, keep the shelves stocked, and help customers. A pharmacist checks the work and answers medicine questions.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Check prescriptions and enter them into the computer.
  • Count, measure, and label medicines.
  • Keep medicines stored safely and stocked.
  • Check deliveries and pull medicine that has expired.
  • Answer phones and help customers at the counter.
  • Send medicine questions to the pharmacist.

The real picture: The work is exact. A small mistake with medicine matters, so every step is checked.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Retail and hospital pharmacies run differently.

  • Morning: Check in a delivery and put medicine in the right places.
  • Later: Enter new prescriptions and count tablets for the pharmacist to check.
  • Midday: Help a line of customers pick up prescriptions.
  • Afternoon: Call an insurance company about a claim, then restock shelves.
  • Before leaving: Clean the counting area and finish the day's records.

Many pharmacies are open evenings and weekends. Hospital pharmacies may be open around the clock.
How You Learn the Job

North Dakota requires training and registration for pharmacy technicians. The North Dakota State Board of Pharmacy says technicians must complete a training program accredited by the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP), either at a school or through an accredited on-the-job program, and pass a national certification exam. Check the board's current rules before you enroll.

  • School programs: North Dakota State College of Science in Wahpeton offers pharmacy technician training. Rasmussen University in Fargo offers an associate degree.
  • Employer programs: Some pharmacies offer accredited on-the-job training. Ask whether a program is accredited before you start.
  • Certification: Plan to study for and pass a national pharmacy technician certification exam.
  • While you train: Ask the board whether you can register as a technician in training while you finish your program.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

Pharmacy technicians in North Dakota register with the State Board of Pharmacy. Ask the board and the employer what you need.

  • An accredited training program, at a school or through an employer.
  • National certification.
  • Registration with the North Dakota State Board of Pharmacy, renewed each year.
  • Continuing education to keep your registration.
  • A background check, which employers usually require.

Before you begin: Ask whether the employer pays for training and the exam, and how long you have to finish.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota pharmacy technician pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $22.86 an hour ($47,560 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $19.89 and $26.08 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $18.45 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $30.70.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 920 of these jobs in 2022. The state projects about 1,030 in 2032, a change of +12%. That works out to about 100 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

These North Dakota projections cover 2022–2032, the newest North Dakota figures shown for this job when checked in October 2026.

Where people work: Drugstores, grocery store pharmacies, hospitals, clinics, and long-term care pharmacies.

Work setting: A pharmacy counter and work area. About 3 in 4 pharmacy technicians say they stand for most of the day.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, shifts, weekends, benefits, paid time off, and whether the employer pays for training and certification.
Where This Can Lead

• Lead technician: Train new technicians and manage stock.
  • Hospital pharmacy: Prepare medicine for hospital patients, sometimes with extra training.
  • Specialty work: Some technicians move into insurance billing, inventory, or pharmacy software.
  • Pharmacist: Becoming a pharmacist takes a doctor of pharmacy degree, which is many more years of school.

Ask your employer whether they help pay for more training.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Being part of healthcare.
  • Clear steps and exact work.
  • Shorter training than many healthcare careers.
  • Pharmacies in many North Dakota towns.

Things to ask about:

  • Standing for most of the shift.
  • Busy rushes and customers who are sick or in a hurry.
  • Evening, weekend, or holiday hours.
  • Training, certification, and yearly registration to keep up.

North Dakota expects about 12% growth, with about 100 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Do you like exact, careful work that helps people stay healthy?

sections: Welcome

A student is stuck on a math problem. A small group needs someone to read with them. A child needs a calm adult nearby. Teacher assistants, often called paraprofessionals or paras, help teachers give students that extra attention.

This career means working closely with students all day. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Teacher Assistant?

You help a teacher in the classroom. You work with students one at a time or in small groups, help keep students safe and on task, and support the teacher's plan. Some assistants work with students who have disabilities.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Help students with lessons one at a time or in small groups.
  • Read aloud and practice skills the teacher has taught.
  • Watch students in classrooms, hallways, lunchrooms, and playgrounds.
  • Help students follow school rules and get along.
  • Get materials ready and help clean up.
  • Talk with the teacher about how students are doing.

The real picture: You are with students almost all day. The teacher plans the lessons, and you help carry them out.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Your day follows the school schedule.

  • Morning: Greet students and help them get settled.
  • Later: Lead a small reading group while the teacher works with others.
  • Midday: Watch students at lunch and recess.
  • Afternoon: Sit beside a student who needs extra help with math.
  • Before leaving: Tell the teacher what went well and what a student found hard.

Some days are calm. Others bring upset students or sudden changes. Staying patient is part of the job.
How You Learn the Job

There is more than one way in. School districts set their own hiring rules, and some jobs have state requirements. Read the actual job ad.

  • Title I paraprofessionals: For jobs paid with Title I funds, North Dakota requires a high school diploma or equivalent plus one of these: two years of college (48 semester hours), an associate degree or higher, or passing a North Dakota-approved test of reading, math, and writing skills.
  • Special education paraprofessionals: North Dakota requires 20 hours of training within the first year on the job. Valley City State, Minot State, and Mayville State universities offer courses that meet this certificate.
  • Optional education: Dakota College at Bottineau and Sitting Bull College in Fort Yates offer teacher assistant associate degrees.
  • On-the-job training: Districts train assistants on school rules, safety, and how to help students.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

Paraprofessional certificates are handled by the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction through NDTeach. Ask the school district which one the job needs.

  • A Title I or special education paraprofessional certificate, depending on the job.
  • A background check, which schools require.
  • Training on student privacy and safety.
  • Some districts ask for first aid or CPR.
  • A teaching license counts in place of the Title I paraprofessional certificate.

Before you begin: Ask what training the district provides and who you go to with questions about a student.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota teacher assistant pay — May 2025 (yearly):

  • Middle pay: $38,240 a year. Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $35,990 and $44,570 a year.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $29,130, and 1 in 10 earned more than $46,260.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 5,260 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 5,600 in 2034, a change of +7%. That works out to about 700 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Public and private schools, preschools, and special education programs across the state.

Work setting: Classrooms, hallways, lunchrooms, and playgrounds. You work close to students and move around much of the day.

Compare an offer: Ask about hourly or yearly pay, hours per day, whether summers are paid, benefits, and paid training.
Where This Can Lead

• Special education assistant: Work closely with students who have disabilities.
  • Special education technician: North Dakota has a technician credential for experienced special education paraprofessionals.
  • Teacher: Some assistants earn a bachelor's degree and a teaching license. Ask about programs for working paraprofessionals.
  • A related direction: Childcare, after-school programs, or youth work.

Working in a school is a good way to find out whether teaching is right for you.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping students learn and grow.
  • A schedule that follows the school year in many jobs.
  • Schools in almost every North Dakota town.
  • A way to try out working in education.

Things to ask about:

  • Pay that is lower than many full-year jobs.
  • Summers that may be unpaid.
  • Students who are upset or have big needs.
  • Being on your feet and moving around all day.

North Dakota expects about 7% growth over ten years, with about 700 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Do you have the patience to help a student keep trying until they get it?
